video_title: Did Crypto's Next Cycle Just Begin?
gist: A Bankless weekly roll-up in which a crypto VC guest argues the August 2026 crypto rally is seller exhaustion plus a liquidity impulse from the Treasury's long-end bond buyback program, which he calls symbolic and says the bond market does not believe. His bigger structural claim is that long-end yields are high because hyperscaler AI debt is crowding out government debt, and that the multi-trillion AI capex bill will ultimately be paid by expanding the money supply — a setup he reads as durably bullish for Bitcoin's dual gold/risk character. Secondary segments dismiss tokenized stocks and Hyperliquid L2s as premature while praising Ethena's token restructuring as a template.

insights.claim: The crypto bear market ended through seller exhaustion rather than new demand: after months of capitulation blog posts and industry exits, the marginal weak hand is gone, and a full cycle had to clear before the next one could begin.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: If the bid is structural exhaustion of supply rather than a news catalyst, dips should be shallower than in the prior 6 months and rallies self-reinforcing.
insights.quote: you need this clearing of a full cycle to give the next cycle permission to begin

insights.claim: Bitcoin's roughly 58K low on June 30 is likely the cycle low, and the speaker sees it as very unlikely that Bitcoin trades below 60K for the rest of the year.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete invalidation level: a sustained break under 60K would falsify the seller-exhaustion thesis and the whole cycle-turn call.
insights.quote: I think it's very unlikely that we tread below 60 this year

insights.claim: Bitcoin rose about 10% on the week to just above 80K, ETH about 7% and Solana about 20%, and the prior week was the largest weekly dollar gain in Bitcoin history at roughly $14K — yet the move only restores prices to approximately May 10 levels.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Frames the rally as a four-month round trip, not a breakout — the year-to-date damage is still unrepaired, which argues against chasing.
insights.quote: last week was the largest weekly dollar gain in Bitcoin history

insights.claim: Prediction-market and options pricing put roughly even odds on Bitcoin ending the year near 60K versus 100K, with visible resistance clustered around the 80K level that the speaker expects Bitcoin to break in one direction rather than sit at.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Symmetric implied distribution around a coiled 80K level favors long volatility/straddle structures over directional spot exposure.
insights.quote: 60K to 100K is roughly even odds of where we end up on the year

themes.theme: The Bessant put and its credibility limits

insights.claim: The 30-year Treasury yield tagged about 5.3% on August 18, a 20-year high, after which Treasury doubled its long-end buybacks from roughly $2 billion to $4 billion per week, and Bessant then framed $4 billion as a floor rather than a cap while officials floated tapping the roughly $950 billion Treasury General Account.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Establishes a de facto reaction function: every approach to ~5.3% on the 30-year has drawn an intervention, giving traders a level to fade or front-run.

insights.claim: The Treasury's long-end buyback program is symbolic rather than flow-relevant: a few billion dollars per week is trivial against Treasury market size, the same way DAT vehicles are too small relative to token trading volumes to actually set prices.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Warns against trading the buyback headline as real yield-curve control — position for yields reverting to their market clearing level, not for a sustained suppressed long end.
insights.quote: the DATs are so small relative to the volumes

insights.claim: The bond market has already rejected the Treasury-put narrative: participants do not believe the TGA will actually be tapped or that authorities will do whatever it takes, so long yields keep yo-yoing back to the level long-term investors demand.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Implies dips in long yields on intervention headlines are sellable, and that a genuine TGA drawdown would be a major surprise repricing.
insights.quote: They don't believe he's going to tap the TGA.

insights.claim: Yield suppression is a threat weapon that loses value the moment it is used: the TGA is a one-time intervention that leaves the Treasury out of bullets, so the tool should be brandished and never actually deployed.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Reframes intervention headlines as bluff maintenance — the bearish tell for bonds would be actual escalation, because it signals the bluff has been called.
insights.quote: the threat is most effective when you don't have to use it

insights.claim: The binding constraint on long yields is not the buyback tool but a roughly $40 trillion debt load and a deficit with no political appetite for austerity — a variable the Treasury Secretary cannot control regardless of tactics.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Argues the term premium is structurally anchored higher, so any yield relief from operations is tactical and mean-reverting.
insights.quote: The real problem is that the debt is too high and the deficit has shows no signs of going down

insights.claim: Stan Druckenmiller publicly rebuked his former protege in a Wall Street Journal op-ed, arguing the long-term Treasury yield is the only fiscal disciplinarian the US has left and that a 30-year clearing at 5.5% is an invoice, not a crisis.
insights.speaker: Stan Druckenmiller (quoted by host)
insights.so_what: A credible macro voice publicly framing suppression as fiscal can-kicking raises the odds of further term-premium expansion and supports debasement hedges.
insights.quote: Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination. If a 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It's an invoice.

insights.claim: The Treasury's announced economic 'D-Day' against Iran — targeting technology, gold, aviation, shipping and digital assets — is unlikely to be enforced to its logical conclusion, because sanctioning Chinese banks ahead of a Xi-Trump summit and into the midterms would inflict economic damage the administration cannot absorb.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Suggests fading headline sanction risk to crypto rails and Chinese bank exposure; the real content is secondary sanctions posturing, not enforcement.
insights.quote: I think the market doesn't buy it. They don't believe that he's actually going to start sanctioning a bunch of Chinese banks.

themes.theme: AI debt crowding out sovereign debt

insights.claim: Long-end government yields are high partly because hyperscalers are issuing debt at unprecedented scale to fund AI capex, directly crowding out Treasuries for a fixed global pool of capital.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Means the term premium is an AI-supply story as much as a fiscal one — it will not compress while capex accelerates, regardless of Treasury operations.
insights.quote: government debt is being crowded out by the hyperscaler debt

insights.claim: Allocators now credibly prefer 30-year hyperscaler paper to 30-year US government paper, because even a 1-3% perceived probability of US default materially raises the yield they demand while Amazon and Meta offer strong cash flows and low leverage.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Frames a relative-value trade — long high-grade hyperscaler credit versus long-duration Treasuries — and explains why sovereign spreads keep widening.
insights.quote: Would I rather buy from, you know, uh, from Amazon and from Meta over 30 years or would I rather buy from the US government?

insights.claim: The 30-year yield has become the main character of all markets because it simultaneously encodes the debasement story and the rising cost of capital that the AI build-out is imposing on everyone else.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Makes the long bond the single chart to monitor for crypto and duration-asset positioning, replacing the Fed policy rate as the key input.

insights.claim: Buying back 30-year bonds and reissuing the debt at shorter maturities is a de facto money-supply expansion, because shorter-duration assets are closer to money — and that added liquidity flows into financial assets including crypto, as it did after COVID.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Gives a mechanical transmission channel from Treasury issuance mix to crypto prices — track the shift in duration of issuance, not just the deficit.
insights.quote: Longer duration assets are less like money. Shorter duration assets are more like money.

insights.claim: Bitcoin is participating in this debasement episode, unlike the earlier gold rally to all-time highs this year that Bitcoin sat out, because Treasury duration transformation stimulates both Bitcoin's gold-like store-of-value character and its risk-asset character at once.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Explains when Bitcoin decouples from gold versus tracks it, and argues this particular macro configuration is the rare one that lifts both legs — so the speaker expects the trend to persist.
insights.quote: It stimulates both the gold-like aspect of Bitcoin as well as the risk asset nature of Bitcoin.

insights.claim: Sell-side and macro voices are explicitly repricing the debasement trade, with a Bernstein call for Bitcoin at 300K within three years and a Fidelity analyst describing a slippery slope toward fiscal dominance that is negative for the dollar and positive for gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Signals the debasement narrative is being institutionalized in research, which tends to bring allocator flows even if the specific price target is noise.
insights.quote: Debasement trade to take Bitcoin to 300K in 3 years

insights.claim: Real onchain RWA demand is in derivatives, not spot: platforms like trade.xyz, Variational and Lighter show far more volume and open interest in RWA perps than the tokenized spot stocks generate in trading volume.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Directs exposure toward perp venues and their tokens rather than tokenized-equity issuers if you want the RWA growth vector.
insights.quote: there's much more demand for the derivatives

insights.claim: Most tokenized stocks are not actual underlying shares but debt instruments that mimic them, fragmented across venues and often priced on capital-inefficient AMMs — one viral example showed roughly 70% slippage on a ~$50K Nvidia purchase.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Execution costs, not regulation, are the binding constraint today — a reason to discount tokenized-equity volume projections and to watch liquidity depth as the real adoption metric.
insights.quote: 70% slippage

insights.claim: Coinbase launching tokenized stocks on Base is the nth entrant into a feature-parity 'me too' category — anyone with a brokerage account already owns stocks, and feature parity is a defensive move that does not grow products, while the genuinely non-substitutable onchain products remain memecoins, NFTs and perps.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: A screening rule for crypto product bets: fund what cannot be done in TradFi, discount what merely replicates it.
insights.quote: Feature parity is a defensive move, not an offensive move.

insights.claim: The tokenized-stock market will take roughly three to four years and will be built by neobanks and fintechs adding dollar-denominated US equities to overseas dollar accounts, because today there are plenty of traders onchain but almost no savers.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Names the actual distribution channel and buyer to watch (offshore dollar savings products), and sets a multi-year clock on the thesis.
insights.quote: there's not a lot of savers on chain right now. There's a lot of traders on chain.

insights.claim: Founders cannot rush market timing: being three steps ahead loses, as with anyone building Hyperliquid in 2018 or building Bancor instead of Uniswap.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: A venture and token-selection filter — right idea at the wrong time is indistinguishable from a wrong idea in returns.
insights.quote: somebody building hyperlquid in 2018 they were just too early, they didn't get to win

insights.claim: The first Zcash ETF is unambiguously good for the protocol and 'ETF shaming' is obsolete, because a genuinely libertarian technology must serve both institutional suits and cypherpunks — and a Grayscale wrapper does not impede shielded usage.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Removes the ideological discount on privacy coins gaining institutional wrappers — a reason to treat privacy-asset ETF listings as straightforwardly bullish.
insights.quote: a truly fully libertarian technology would allow both suits and cipher punks to use it at the same time

insights.claim: HyperEVM underperformed expectations because it was genuinely slow with unpredictable fees, since Hyperliquid prioritizes throughput for HyperCore's exchange — and building an L1 requires a different skill set than building a great perp exchange, which is the gap a new collocated L2 (Alisium, from the team behind Connect) is trying to fill using HYPE as gas, the order book as a native oracle, and opcodes exposing full order-book depth rather than only top of book.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Explains why HYPE ecosystem bets on smart-contract activity have disappointed, and identifies real-time order-book depth onchain as the one genuinely new primitive to evaluate.
insights.quote: it had just in raw terms actually very bad performance. It was very slow.

insights.claim: The Hyperliquid L2 will probably fail to bootstrap an ecosystem because users come to Hyperliquid to trade perps rather than to build, most founders who tried HyperEVM already got burned, and most L2s do not survive — with liquid staking protocol Kinetic the notable exception trying to muscle an ecosystem into existence.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Bearish on the HYPE-ecosystem-expansion trade; capital is better placed in the perp franchise itself than in the app layer around it.
insights.quote: People are on Hyperlid to trade PES. That's why they're there.

insights.claim: Ethena executed a full token restructuring in one move — buying out early investors who had been selling ENA over the prior nine months, eliminating monthly VC unlocks, assigning IP and protocol value exclusively to a foundation under token-holder control so equity investors have no residual cash flow claim, and putting a fee switch to a live governance vote — and the token rose about 20% on the day.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A concrete, priced-in template: the market paid roughly 20% for removing structural sell pressure and aligning equity with the token.

insights.claim: Liquid funds refused to buy ENA despite liking the product purely because of recurring monthly unlocks and visible dumping — they would not stand in front of known supply, meaning the discount was structural rather than fundamental.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Identifies unlock overhang as a screenable, removable discount — tokens with good products and heavy vesting schedules are candidates for the same re-rating.
insights.quote: these types of investors, they ultimately are just like this ball and chain

insights.claim: Ranking the drivers of the re-rating, the speaker guesses buying out the sellers and unlocking everyone mattered most, unifying equity with the token second, and the fee switch least — while acknowledging the changes were bundled so causation cannot be isolated.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Suggests weighting supply-overhang removal above cash-flow switches when screening tokens for restructuring upside — and that future copycats will provide the cleaner data if they stagger changes.
insights.quote: probably taking out the sellers and unlocking everyone was a big part of it

insights.claim: The restructuring was only possible because the SEC changed its posture on whether tokens are securities, ending the era in which projects contorted their structures to avoid regulatory fury.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Regulatory change is the enabling condition for a broad wave of token restructurings — the trade is anticipating which legacy tokens clean up their cap tables next.

insights.claim: Restructuring cannot rescue tokens without product-market fit — turning on a fee switch is meaningless if there are no fees, and most imitators will simply be putting lipstick on a pig.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Filter the coming copycat wave by underlying revenue and product traction; buy the restructuring only where the protocol already earns real fees.
insights.quote: I should go put lipstick on my pig

themes.theme: AI capital supercycle and its real constraints

insights.claim: AI capex is climbing a capital ladder — hyperscalers first burned retained earnings, then moved to Wall Street credit as with the $500 billion Nvidia deal, and sovereign credit appears to be next, with Dylan Patel's estimate of roughly $1 trillion this year, $2 trillion by 2028 and as much as $11 trillion by 2030.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Quantifies the funding gap and identifies the escalation path — each rung up the ladder raises the global cost of capital and pressures long-duration assets.
insights.quote: by 2030, we may need as much as 11 trillion in AI capex

insights.claim: AI labor is the successor to human population growth as civilization's reinvestment engine: global fertility has peaked so human labor is capped, and capital will now compound into building AI labor the way it once compounded into growing the human population.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Justifies treating AI capex as structurally reflexive and open-ended rather than a capex cycle with a natural top — the key reason the speaker stays bullish through volatility.
insights.quote: human labor is tapped. This is all the human labor we're ever going to get. AI labor is going to be where human civilization grows.

insights.claim: The trillions needed for AI will come mainly from creating new money rather than reallocating existing capital, and this is legitimate under the speaker's view that fiat money is a social fiction which only works when everyone agrees the future will hold more goods than the past — a belief AI-driven real growth would justify.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: The single most tradeable claim in the episode: it makes long AI and long debasement hedges (crypto, gold, scarce assets) the same trade rather than competing ones, with realized productivity growth the test of whether the expansion is benign.
insights.quote: probably we're going to create new money. Probably it's going to be an expansion of the money supply

insights.claim: Anthropic is expected to go public later this year, and having a frontier lab in public markets will produce extreme volatility because the stock will trade on society's collective fears and imagination — the speaker calls it the most feared company he has ever seen.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: A dateable catalyst: a listed frontier lab creates a new high-beta AI instrument and a volatility transmission channel into every correlated AI and risk asset.
insights.quote: anthropics going public later this year, almost certainly

insights.claim: Local data-center backlash is not a real constraint because compute can relocate to Canada, Mexico, Malaysia or offshore at the cost of a little latency — the genuine risk is governments running out of rope, seen already in export controls and the Commerce Department blocking model releases, with a step change in model capability and therefore in regulatory response coming soon.
insights.speaker: guest, crypto VC
insights.so_what: Reprioritizes AI-trade risk monitoring away from NIMBY headlines toward national-security and model-release policy, which is where a showstopping shock would originate.
insights.quote: It's running out of rope with governments

insights.claim: Even if the decade-long AI thesis is correct, the path will not be a straight line — like Bitcoin's journey toward gold-scale market cap it should proceed through leverage-driven booms and busts, and the fact that AI financing has already reached the sovereign bond market suggests this era's capital pool is nearing its limit.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Argues for owning the secular AI and debasement exposure while sizing for a violent interim drawdown once the cost of capital bites.
